utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; fellow counsellors; good morning, Brigadier. Before I recommence with my examination-in-chief, we have this morning supplied to the Chamber some translations of extracts of the report document. I went through the document with a language assistant yesterday afternoon. It was a very hurried exercise, but we tried to identify points that were perhaps amplifying what was in the original statement and have those specifically translated whilst the translators work on the full document to provide it to Your Honours at the earliest opportunity. As I say, my learned friends for the Defence have the full document in their own language anyway. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we had shown you a few documents in relation to the questioning regarding general matters of military strategy, military conduct, and the actions and obligations of commanders. I would like you to look, indeed, at the documents attached to your statement again, sir, and, in fact, pick document number AD1.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, I understand this is not a controversial document in terms of ever being before any Chamber before. It is a fresh document. That is obviously conceded, but I think that's its status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you look at that document, and could you tell me what that conveys to you as regards a military communication? What is it, and from what level of person does it pass, and to what level of person does it go to?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, to begin with. AD1 is the example of a report. The commander of a company sends his report to the commander of the military police, and this document is correct in all its aspects. The only thing that is not correct, militarily speaking, is that one step had been skipped. He should have sent it to the battalion commander, and then the battalion commander should then send it on to the commander of the military police. So one rung had been skipped. We do not have a battalion commander here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, does the document, on the face of it, indicate what company issued that report?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. In my analysis, I also quoted a example; what reports, orders, and everything else should look like and what they should contain. Reports and orders do not have to include all the basic points, but they must comply with the principal point; that is, the name of the unit or the institution issuing the report, the reference number, the filing number, date, and the addressee. These are the principal elements. Then, of course, the signature of the person who has written the report, and the seal. These are the most important elements of both orders and reports. Of course, the contents may vary and may include the elements which are expected to be included in every report and every order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so just looking at the document, does that tell you, on the face of the document, from whom it was sent? Who sent it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was sent by a company commander, and it is addressed to the military police command. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which company is that? Does it say, on the face of it, which company he is the commander of?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is correct here. The 1st Active Company of the military police, 4th Battalion. So the heading says that it is a unit which is called 1st Active Company, part of the 4th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, as to the identity of that company commander -- clearly you'd not previously seen this document -- I appreciate that fact; you don't know its contents -- but what appears to be the name of the company commander on that report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. We object to this. It is not true that the witness did not see this report. The witness did see this report. That is my yesterday's objection to the documents presented to this witness earlier without having been authenticated in this court as authentic documents. Now questions take all this information about the company person, who might have written this, and so on and so forth. So do I not really think that what my learned friend said is correct, that the witness did not see this. Yes, he did see these documents, and he supplied his answer in an earlier document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's not an objection to your question, but the way you phrased your question. Counsel Pavkovic is correct in saying that the witness did see the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What I was trying to get to, in a simple way -- and I think I made a mess of it, Your Honour -- is simply that this man is not the author of the document, and I'm trying to express that he, obviously, is not able to speak as to the truth of its contents or indeed the fact of it being signed by whoever it purports. I'm just dealing with the face of the document: "As an expert looking at it, does it look like a military document, and what do you see there?" and it bears no more weight than that, but I suggest it is admissible and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, yes, Brigadier, again I would just ask you to confirm. You see a signature block on that document. I'm just asking you to say that on the face of it, of that document that you saw, who appears to be the signatory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The commander of that company. I do not know that individual, but what it says is "company commander," and then typed "Vladimir Santic." Of course, I cannot claim this is his signature. That is only what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier. I would like you to turn now to documents AD2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: These are contentious documents in some measure, Your Honours. I'm wondering whether, out of an abundance of caution -- although hopefully my questions will not create a problem -- that we would have private session for about five minutes, just to be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then next, if you please, Brigadier, would you be so kind as to look at your documents AD5 and 6. Now, looking at document AD5, Brigadier, could you please again -- please do not necessarily refer to any names in it; that's not relevant to us -- but can you tell us what the nature of document AD5 is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Document AD5 is basically an order, a short one, because the preamble says: Pursuant to the order of the commander of the 4th military police battalion number such-and-such of 2nd April, I order or designate. So it is a form, a type of a short order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would an order of that nature -- firstly, may I ask you -- sorry, sir. Does that order appear to be drawn up in a proper military fashion, according to your knowledge of these things?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I have said it. In principle, there is a pattern for orders, for decisions, for reports and what they should contain, in principle, all these orders and reports and decisions. But I also mentioned yesterday, if you remember, that an order may be in one sentence only if circumstances so require. So it may depend on the situation. What is important is that they contain all these elements: who it is addressed to, who it is sent by, and the date and the number. And, of course, the contents may vary depending on the circumstances, on the conditions, so that there may be only one item, there may be various items, but, I mean, whatever is necessary for the task to be then carried out. But in this specific case, I believe this suffices if it only means that certain soldiers are assigned as assistants. So it is a list of soldiers, and that suffices for the task for the order to be carried out properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This order assigning these various people, again, can you say from which company or battalion that is coming, and who is to be the signatory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This order, too, comes from the 1st Active Company of the military police in Vitez, and it is signed by a commander. Or, rather, the order was written here, the principle of the chain of command was complied with, so it is the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is the signatory to this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The signatory is the company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name you see on that document, the signatory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Vladimir Santic is what is typed here, and the signature itself, Santic, whether that is his signature, that is something that I cannot say. But in typed letters it is Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Document AD6, sir. Again, would you just tell us what is that document? Is that an order or some other form of document? And what does it instruct people to do, or what does it report upon?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This is a typical order, or a short order, and it was written pursuant to the order issued by the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, so that this chain of command principle was complied with in this case too. Here this designates -- there is units of the 1st Company which are sent out to carry out a specific mission. In the second -- the second item, then, specifies that the AT Platoon will be ensuring the safety of persons and premises according to the instructions of the commander of the company, and I can't really read this properly. So the second item, it says that: AT Platoon members shall provide the safety for the personnel and the facilities under the instructions of the commander of the 2nd Company of the 4th Battalion. So the AT Platoon is to provide security for persons on the basis of the instructions of the commander of the 2nd Company. So the AT Platoon of the 1st Company was, in this particular case, assigned to the commander of the 2nd Company to then provide the security for individual persons under his instructions. And the important thing here, in the fifth item, after the order has been complied with, men should be transferred to the seat of the unit in an organised manner. This is a logical order, both as regards the addressee and the signature; that is, the commander of the 4th Battalion, and there is -- then the commander of the 2nd Company of the 4th Battalion, the commander of the AT platoon, and one for the files. So the specific thing is the commander of 2nd Company is here charged with providing the security according to the instructions of the commander of the 2nd Company. So this is a type of an attachment of the AT Platoon to the commander of the 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, using the expression "attachment," do you see from this whether it is a long-term duty or a short-term duty, the attachment of these people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Here we have the date and the day when the AT Platoon is placed at the disposal of the 2nd Company commander of the 2nd Company of the military police. I do not see really for how long they are assigned to him, and I can't see that. Perhaps it does say somewhere, but I don't remember seeing it, how long they are assigned to that particular mission. Perhaps there is somewhere else, but it doesn't say here clearly. There is no time frame. One doesn't know for how long this AT Platoon will be at the disposal of the 2nd Company commander. All we see here is that after the mission has been accomplished, the men of the platoon should be transferred to the headquarters of the unit, but how long the task is to take, it doesn't say here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, finally, in respect to those documents, again, Brigadier, can you say from which company those -- or within which those orders were made and who made those orders? Who was the signatory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The order was drawn up by the 1st Active Company of the 4th Battalion of the military police, and the order was signed by the company commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you say the name that appears on the piece of paper just appears to be the commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: "Company commander," and then it is typed "Vladimir Santic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Brigadier, have you, in the course of your military duties in around the time, made any study of the events that occurred in Ahmici, in the Lasva Valley, on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, more specifically I was the head of the staff of the 1st Corps in Sarajevo, and my -- and that particular area of responsibility was not part of my terms of reference; that is, it was not an area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. But since -- as of August 1993, the general headquarters of the then-army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the present commander Army of the Federation, at that time I was the head of the planning administration; that is, the operative administration. At that administration we received all the reports, both from our unit -- that is, units directly subordinate to us of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and the reports which were -- which presented some interest to us from the military point of view, and we were receiving them from other units, from all the other areas of responsibility, so that I can say that I was conversant with the situation because of that. And with my HVO colleagues, I always discussed those matters, because we both attended various meetings; and during the negotiations, while the conflict was under way, we often attended various training meetings, drills, courses, et cetera, et cetera, and soldiers just naturally always discussed such areas as Ahmici and other areas which are of interest to us. So for that reason, I do know the situation in that area and throughout the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre of war, because I had all the information in one place, both in relation to the army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO and the BH army, so that I can really say that I'm conversant with the situation -- that I was conversant with the situation as much as it was possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Brigadier, could you offer, from your knowledge of what you say you believe happened in Ahmici -- would you, firstly, indicate what forces you think were involved?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to apologise for having to speak -- to take the floor once again. This witness was called in to testify as an expert witness. The witness has no experience or direct knowledge of what happened in Ahmici. Now, this information the witness is referring to, the experience and everything else, to my mind, it goes beyond an expert testimony, and I object to this. I do not think that the examination should go on in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll explain the purpose of the next few questions. It's virtually the last element of my examination-in-chief. As I understand the role of the expert, it would be a position, Your Honours, that we would -- an expert receives information and, upon the information, is then able to form, one hopes, with the expertise they profess, an opinion to offer. Now, clearly, I feel it appropriate, if I'm going to ask matters which are generally about the organisational requirements and the level of coordination and so forth required in an operation such as the 16th of April, it would be appropriate, obviously, to see what perception the expert has, because then Your Honours will know the factual basis upon which he bases his opinion. If his facts are wrong, then you know what weight to give his opinion. If his facts are right, then, likewise, you'll know the foundation upon which he makes those opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We uphold the objection of Counsel Pavkovic. I think Counsel Pavkovic is right. He's going to guess. He can't guess, the witness. So I wonder whether you could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. Just give me a moment; I'll cull my questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just now to deal with one final theoretical matter, Brigadier, not related to any specific actual event, but if, if a company was to be deployed in the field in a combat operation and involves three or four platoons and maybe other units of an army, what kind of level of planning and coordination is required of the commanders, particularly at company level? Please, you can be as brief as possible, because the general principles you've already covered.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: What can a company commander do if he gets a concrete task and if he has three or four platoons or squads available? Well, yesterday I explained a few elements. Specifically, a company commander calls in his commanders; that is to say, platoon commanders. He familiarises them with the task that lies ahead, he points out which are the really important elements for carrying out this task, and then, if the conditions are right, he goes out to the ground to specifically outline the tasks he gave on the ground. I already explained that this can be done from one location if the specific situation permits this and all the commanders can be present. However, if this is a wider area, then he can use his own judgement, his own assessment, to see which unit should be used where, and then he can show each and every commander what he should do. So these are the tactics that are usually applied. We always point out, in military theory and practice, that the best thing is to issue tasks on the ground, because maps, written documents, in general, have their shortcomings when compared to a concrete situation that can be directly seen. Therefore, the best thing is to issue assignments on the ground. In military practice, it is very well known that this is the best way of issuing orders and having them carried out. In this connection, it is important to coordinate activities with regard to all elements, in terms of logistics; communications; carrying out the task itself, whether it will be carried out in one stage, in two stages, in several stages; et cetera. That is to say that a commander is kept very busy. He has many activities related to carrying out such a task. Finally, when all of that is coordinated, when every one of his subordinates gets a specific assignment, then the company commander is engaged, together with his team, in elaborating certain combat documents. Combat documents are made so that everyone would know, for several reasons, what each and every unit does, what kind of activity it is engaged in. This is done for the sake of history, for the sake of archives. So it is envisaged, for each and every combat action, to have these combat documents made. Usually, at company level, a decision is made as to how a specific assignment will be carried out. A schematic is made, and then one can see how each and every unit will be deployed, the depth and the breadth of every task can seen on the map. Then one can see whether this unit can carry out that particular assignment independently or whether it seeks artillery support or the support of some other unit. In most cases concerning specific tasks, not a single unit has, within its own organic composition, all the elements that would make it possible for it to carry out such a task. Then a commander can ask his superior to have an entire artillery, engineering, et cetera, unit attached to him, or part of such a unit, in order to carry out a specific task. In this connection, the commander carries out all these activities I mentioned, and then, if at all possible, he goes to check out, in practice, how his order or decision is carried out on the ground; that is, before combat operations begin. But I pointed out yesterday that when combat operations begin, the company commander should be at such a location that makes it possible for him to have the best conditions possible for monitoring the situation so that he can change, correct, if necessary, alter his decisions, depending on the situation on the ground, what the new elements may be that he was unfamiliar with and what the problems are that he could not have forecast before that. When doing that, he does this in certain time intervals and then provides reports to his superior officers on everything he's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That concludes my questions. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sorry to pre-empt my friend for a second. I would like to, in fact, formally to tender, in due course, the statement and the report prepared. I advise Your Honours in advance of that. Obviously, the full report with translation will be in your hands -- we have part of the translation submitted this morning -- just lest I forget at a later point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection, Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood the Prosecutor correctly, he is going to offer a statement; that is to say, he is going to tender the statement that I spoke about yesterday and the report I spoke about yesterday. Did I understand you correctly? Oh, I did. Well, I have certain objection with regard to the first document, and I think it should not be included because the expert had documents made available to him by the Prosecutor, and they would not have been accessible to this expert had the Prosecutor not disclosed this to him. However, I do not have any objections with regard to the second document that was mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Our ruling is that both documents should be admitted into evidence, both the statement with the annexes and the document which will be circulated in English, in extenso, maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. We hope to have that ready tomorrow, Your Honours. My only other observation at this point would be an abundance of caution, now, after Your Honours' observations of yesterday, and that is, perhaps should that document, because of the annexures, be filed as confidential or something. Just particularly I'm thinking AD2 to 4, where I think that is particularly relevant, if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So they will be confidential. Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be the first to examine the witness, and then after that it will be Ranko Radovic, Luka Susak, and Petar Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement of the witness will be 310, Prosecution evidence; and the report 311, also Prosecution evidence. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Witness. My name is Petar Pavkovic, Attorney at Law. Yesterday and today you expressed a very fair assessment of military doctrine, the chain of command, and other doctrinary matters, and I thank you for having helped me to put my questions today perhaps in a better way, thanks to your testimony. However, I would like you to clarify certain matters to me a bit. First of all, you're a Brigadier, from what I've been able to see, but you are a Brigadier-General in terms of the formation post that you hold. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any wartime experience? In this last war, I mean, this last war that was waged in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned the initial period; that is to say, April 1992. I was in the republican -- rather, I received instructions from the territory of defence headquarters in Sarajevo to help the establishment of the Territorial Defence in Konjic, because this was the very inception of the Territorial Defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina, generally speaking, and it was also the very inception of this new army. My first task or, rather, my first experience was in the area of Visoko, when, in the month of June, we tried -- that's the way I have to put it -- to deblockade a certain area that led to Sarajevo via Visoko and Vares, and then I was commander of the tactical group of Visoko, of Vares. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about June; is that right? Which year?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That was 1992. And then in August 1992, I was head of the staff in the temporary command of South 92. That is also an operation which was planned for the purposes of deblockading Sarajevo, because the general purpose was always this deblockade. I don't want anybody to be confused by this. And how realistic this was is another matter. But this was this other operation where I was chief of staff from the broader area of Igman. That's where the deblockade of Sarajevo was supposed to be carried out. And then as chief of staff of the 1st Sarajevo Corps, I had a series of wartime experience in the units of the 1st Corps. So that is where I was directly engaged in the operations; that is to say, I was directly engaged as an officer according to the post I held. Later, as chief of administration for operations and planning, I was not in a position to be directly engaged in these operations, to directly participate, because this was not the post I held. But often I went to Vlasic, Igman, Treskavica, Kupres. Also the areas of Prenj, Bjelasnica, et cetera; that is to say, those areas that were accessible at the time, and those units as well. Because that was my duty, after all. This element of control was necessary, in terms of our planned activities. So I was actually checking up on these planned activities that we had envisaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You took part in this as a member of the TO or, rather, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you fighting against?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: At that time, in 1992 -- that is to say, until the conflict with the HVO broke out -- we had one enemy only, and that was the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be more concise. Did you take part in the fighting against the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. No. Not directly. Not directly. I was not directly in such a position. I was in such a position only in terms of taking up on certain planned activities. When I came to Kakanj, where our general staff had been transferred at the time -- you are probably familiar with that -- that was January 1994, and in that period I carried out planned activities in the territory of Central Bosnia and in other territories that were accessible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one may infer that in a certain way, in accordance with the position you held in the chain of command in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did take part in operations in respect of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You can't put it that way. I pointed this out at the very outset. My direct participation was when I was commander or, rather, chief of staff. And when I became, in 1993, the chief of administration for operative planning, I did not have anything directly to do with combat activity; that is to say, I wrote and drew things. So perhaps this makes it clearer to you. That is to say that we, from the general staff, from the highest level of command, we issued appropriate orders and commands. It was only normal. And that was my function in that respect, not direct participation in a unit that was engaged in fighting. We have to make a distinction between the two; that is to say, not only I, but the function of the general staff as a general staff is such. So the general staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at the time, did not directly participate in any such thing at all. That was the function of all other staffs, not only the army staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we treat only the rank-and-file soldiers as direct participants, then of course you did not take part in any combat activities. But you will agree with me that military planning, the issuing of orders, is also part of overall combat activity that is carried out vis-a-vis the other side. And the lower units, as you explained to us yesterday, did not carry out their own tasks, but the tasks given to them by higher levels of command. So, in accordance with the principles of command that you explained to us yesterday, you nevertheless, in a way which is compliant with your role, did take part in the operations that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Croatian Defence Council units? Please, could you briefly give me a "yes" or a "no" answer, but we really have to move on.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The function of a staff and the function of a commander are very, very different functions. Only a commander -- and that's the way it is everywhere -- has the right to command; that is to say, the commander, who is a person -- or rather, a person who is called a commander has the right to issue commands. And he is responsible. He is the only one who is responsible for everything that happens. Rasim Delic, at that time commander of the general staff, was responsible for the entire army. The commander of the corps was responsible for the entire corps, but not people from the staff too. That is to say that I cannot sign an order, I cannot have responsibility as chief of administration. It is only the commander that signs a command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. VRDOLYAK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is a mistake in the transcript. Instead of "headquarters," it says "staff." It should be the function of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We'll get it straight. May I ask the witness to be concise and specific, not to indulge in generalities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, perhaps you misunderstood me. It is not my intention to establish your responsibility or something. I just wanted to see where your position was, and I am satisfied with the answer you've given so far. So let us move a step forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. VRDOLYAK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, again there is a mistake here. Instead of "staff," it should say "headquarters." The word "staff" can mean both staff and headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's either a building or people, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is the explanation from the interpreters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained to us the chain of command, you explained subordination to us, you explained the unity of command. You spoke of the chain of command and you said that lower units or, rather, the commanders of lower-level units, had a certain degree of freedom and initiative, but that this freedom of theirs has to move within the fundamental ideas of the commander. So if an attack order was issued from a higher level, it can never be understood as a defence order, if one strictly respects hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Would you like me to answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please say whether I understood you well and whether I said this correctly.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: You did understand me correctly, but it's not only lower-level unit commanders. Every subordinate officer has initiative within those boundaries that you have referred to; that is to say, to formulate certain ideas that do not deviate from the general objective. However, if he does this, he has to inform his superior officer that he assessed the situation, that he has more information, and that he believes that the order can be carried out in a different way. But basically that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me, when we speak about combat activities, that combat activities are a series of activities that can be divided, essentially, into attack activities and defence activities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: According to strategy, there is a strategic offensive -- that's the expert word for it -- and strategic defence. And within strategic defence there are all forms of attack and attack activities; and within defence, strategic defence, all forms of defensive activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that within defence activities or defence, strategically speaking, certain activities can have the characteristics of offensive activities? What is active defence, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is also one of the principles. And there is a term "active defence." That means that part of a unit is used exclusively for defence, and another part of the unit is used for offensive activities, for various attacks, ambushes, et cetera. When we say that within strategic defence -- if we look at the highest level, what is the determining factor, whether this is an attack or a defence, or offensive or defensive, it is the number of units engaged. If the predominant number of units in that zone are engaged in defence activities, then it is defence, but if the predominant number of units in that zone is engaged in attack in that zone, and according to that task, then it is offensive. But in the context of offensive and defensive activities, there can be both kinds, and the determining factor is whether a larger number is involved in defence or attack. And if most are engaged in attack, then it's a typical attack, and if a larger number of units are in defence, then it's typical defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that I can also see from relevant documents for an attack and for a defence, because those who are assessing the strength of a particular unit will also decide whether it will go into an attack or a defence, or whether they will be engaged in some other form of operations. So that documents also allow us to see what kind of operations are addressed there, unless they have personal experience in this.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. If a corps commander is organising the defence by the whole unit, then the whole unit are only -- all the units or only parts of the corps may go into it. So within the general task, within the overall task, the strength or either the number of the -- of units of men and equipment will determine whether something will be a defence action or an offensive action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about the command, leadership in the Yugoslav People's Army, with which you spent a major part of your career, and you tried to draw a comparison or, rather, to juxtapose the principles of leadership and command in there and in the armies which came about in Bosnia-Herzegovina entities. And you asserted that these principles were embraced, more or less successfully, in all the three armies; that is, the Army of the Republika Srpska, HVO and Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You also indicated certain differences between them and you told us why did these differences exist. Could you tell us now if these principles which were adopted not only by the former JNA and quite a number of the armies we went over, was it all that simple to adopt them and put them through in the newly established armies, in view of the shortage of, shall I say, properly qualified officer cadres and other personnel?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Listen. I mean, the principles are such as you have just said, and that applies to all the armies in the world; all of them are governed by these principles. And, yes, we did embrace that. I mean, all the three armies. But it was easiest for the Army of the Republika Srpska because the available equipment, armament, literature, war plans and everything else went to one people. So it was easiest for the Army of the Republika Srpska to accept it or take it over and reorganise. And then -- because in Croatia, what happened, it was the next -- easier for the HVO, because they were receiving some assistance from Croatia, as was only natural. And it was least easy for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina because it had the least equipment and other material and everything else, which of course affects this. The question of the qualified personnel, qualified commanding personnel, is of crucial importance. And that applied to all three armies regarding the organisation and formation of all armies, especially at the initial stage in 1992. It was difficult to apply the system of leadership and command, but it was applied because it cannot be any other way. In spite of the differences, it was difficult to apply in those cases where the commanders, for some reason, a justified reason, were designated. And the commander may be a civilian as well, if somebody appointed him to that particular duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at the theory, then the HVO rules at that time, if we juxtapose them to JNA rules, also upheld the same standards, but in practice these principles could not be upheld at the same level, because on the one hand we had an army which was developing its structure, which had been developing its structure for 40 years, and the latter had been in existence for only one year.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite true. But we were all faced with problems of that kind, that we appointed commanders by their full name, even if they were not professional officers or soldiers until that time. But in all these organisations and formations that we had, there were also career soldiers, professional soldiers, who lent a hand to these people. And schools and courses began shortly afterwards through the HVO, the Army of BH and elsewhere; that is, courses to train such people. That was the process and that was quite a natural operation. So that is true; it is quite true that it was difficult to apply in practice the leadership and command system as it is postulated by theory. But our rules also say, and I can see that it was everywhere, that ignorance does not relieve your responsibility. That is the certain rules. It does not relieve you of responsibility, regardless of what he is talking about. In our practice, we often said that. Somebody says, "I'm not a lawyer. I didn't know this or that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, I must ask you, and I will try to cut my questions short, and I should also like you -- to ask you to be concise. I do not wish to interrupt you, but, still, could you please take care? Yesterday you spoke about your personal experience as regards the military police. You are an infantryman, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about the military police, in theory?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In practice, our unit often included the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. I was the commander of the brigade staff, but within my personnel we also had a military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said, and I quote: "The military police reluctantly conducts defence operations." You presented that as your personal experience.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was the military police or any other unit -- does the military police or any other unit do what it likes or what it is ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, they do what they're ordered to do, but they're special units: reconnaissance, military police, subversive, and so on and so forth. In principle they were treated as units which could do -- which was beyond some other units. In that sense they were some special units, and, therefore, they did what --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, otherwise, they are also subjected and bound to comply with the orders they're issued?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it within the terms of reference of the military police in wartime -- and in peacetime as well, but in wartime perhaps more -- providing security of the command post? Is that an important task of the military police; that is, are they there to provide the security for documents, for the records, and the commander? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is one of its duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I went through the rules that you submitted, and I could see it says, on page 33 of the document: "Military police in wartime carries out the tasks as follows: (A) ..." First it says: "Directly provide the security the command post, the commander of the military unit, and institution in -- at its seat or when -- or on the move, and military couriers who carry military documents of the highest confidentiality." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but I did not really list all the tasks, but I think I say somewhere -- and all the other orders issued it. That, I think, go for all the armies in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But regardless of its other activities, this is also one of the very important tasks of the military police, which cannot --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is one of the regular tasks of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you enclosed with your expert opinion an example of an order for -- of an attack order, and I believe you have it with you, a fragment of it.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, a fragment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you please help me to briefly go through these general principles of an attack order? Witness, tell me -- it is page 216 of your document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here you give us a fragment and you begin with item 4 of such an attack order. Now, according to these definitions -- that is, which forces, which directions, which objectives -- and we recognise that this is an attack order, even if we did not have a heading which said that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is quite true what it says here, that it is an attack on main forces and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to show what a specific combat order would look like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then item 5. Item 5, you also say what this particular mission of the 1st Company looks like.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then item 6 for the 2nd Company; and item 7, 3rd company.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see the objective of the attack, because we have directions of their movement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a complete pattern, model of what an order should look like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Why didn't you also show us a defence order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, because it is identical. This thing is quite identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what is the difference?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, the only difference is that it says "defence" instead of "attack." So here he says -- and the defence order here says the area of attack, and it will say area of attack, and it will say the area of defence. So that would be the only distinction. And just as the combat operations, the role and place of the commander, they're always the same, regardless of whether it's attack or defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you briefly explain what would a defence order look like?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, if you have them here, I can go through all these items -- there's seven -- if you like. So instead of "armoured unit in the area of attack," it will say the same unit in the area of defence, the depth, the width of the front, and the mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what does it mean when an order says preparedness at such-and-such hour on a particular date?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It means, in all cases, in all instances, that a unit must be prepared for that task at a given time, but it may happen that this particular mission begins later. But that is a set time by which I, as a commander, must prepare my unit so that it can set off to carry out its mission. But whether we shall set off to conduct that mission, that may be changed by my superior, and, say, instead of 6.00, it will start at 7.00, or for some reason, objective reasons, it will start earlier. But that, of course, you transmit that change down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, all the combat -- all the things have to be completed and the unit must be fully combat-prepared and waiting for the sign to go into an operation.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what is done by professional soldiers, and they know that. Sometimes they do not even write down the preparedness, and that is not a mistake, but that is basically what preparedness means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should only briefly like to go through documents we were shown yesterday. So could you please -- could we go into private session, please, for a short while?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted) 21 (redacted) 22 (redacted) 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, Witness, when asked by the Prosecution, you analysed documents in Annex A and marked as AD1 to AD6, and you said that you were reading there the signature of the commander, and you mentioned his name. You do not know if that is the signature of the person indicated here as the commander of that company?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Quite true. I have never seen that person. I've never seen his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these documents AD2, AD3, and AD4, that these were not combat orders?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are sorry; they could not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please answer this question?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Perhaps you did not hear it. I apologise. The first three documents -- these first documents are not combat orders; they are orders relative to disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the document AD5, even if it says that it is minutes, you established -- you asserted that it was an order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Quite right. It cannot be minutes of anything. So this is an example. As soon as you see -- as soon as you see the words "odredjujem" or "odlucujem," it means, "I thereby determine, or order, or I decide." As soon as you have these three words, "I command, I order, I decide," then it is an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. That is from the point of view of everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean from the point of view of the doctrine?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, every soldier will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but other people --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, with that, of course, a reservation. I mean -- but a soldier would know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but a person who is not a professional soldier may do that out of sheer ignorance?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I already told you -- I mean, it may -- it may happen so, and even in mathematics, sometimes the solution is not correct but it gives you the best result. But what it says here, this is an order, because it says "designate here," and this was in how many -- with the order of the commander of the 4th Battalion. So he could not do anything else. So this is an order really, because it does say here, "Pursuant to the order of the commander." You told me to carry out this particular task, and then I contact the immediate executors and tell them to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But it, nevertheless, says here that it is nothing but a list.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The list is only a preamble, but we see where these soldiers are going to. So this list is -- the list could have been an annex to the document. The list could have been an annex to the order; that is, the order could have come down to only the sentence. "The soldiers are going to reinforce Travnik," and that could have been the order, the whole of the order, and then attached to it could have been the list of these people here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have only one question more. Will you please look at the document under A6, and that is the document of the 8th of April, 1993. Could you please confirm it for us that this document does not show how long will this unit be attached to the commander of the 2nd Company?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I believe I did confirm that I could not see that period of time. One sees when it is to be -- when it is being attached to the commander of the 2nd Company, but I could not read anywhere for how long it would be attached to it. It does not appear here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, when was this order issued?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1993. And on the 8th of April. So it should have been before 12.00. Before 12.00, sometime in the morning hours, so that this company -- so that this unit could carry out this task; that is, the unit must be prepared to carry out its task on this day when the order is issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. So we now take the usual 30-minute break, and then we resume with Counsel Radovic, Susak, and Puliselic. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will resume with Counsel Radovic. May I ask Counsel Radovic, Counsel Susak and Counsel Puliselic to try to be as brief as possible, because we would like to start with the next witness, if possible. And then at the end of this testimony we will do some planning for the future, and you will see why we are keen to move on quickly. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Ranko Radovic. I am one of the Defence counsel of the accused Zoran Kupreskic, as the first defendant. I will first start with the documents that the Prosecutor showed you, and I would like to ask you to have a look at AD8. We are talking about the order issued on the 15th of April at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner it says where this order came from. So could you please give us the place that this order came from?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The command headquarters of the operative zone of Central Bosnia forward, the command post -- oh, forward command post. Yes, forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Forward command post, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, operative zone, that's in the HVO. Which formation was that? Was it like a corps?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was a formation similar to a corps; a division, a corps, approximately that rank, that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was below the level of operative -- what was below the level of operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was battalions and brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the right-hand side -- in the upper right-hand corner, "defence military secret."

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: "Strictly confidential."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean when it says "defence military secret, strictly confidential" on a document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That means that that document is handed over only to persons who are in charge. That is to say that only persons who are in charge within the chain of command are supposed to familiarise themselves with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain this. It starts from the command of the operative zone or a corps, and then who would be the person in charge who would get this order?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, it says here who it was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please stop overlapping the witness, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is customary that it is sent from the operative zone to the brigade, and from the brigade to the battalion; that is, within the operative brigade. But it can also go independently to an independent battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. To which level of command would this first order go?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: This first order should go to the first level. That is the principle. That should be received by the commander of the brigade and commander of the independent battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this first order? Would the brigade commander give it further to battalions, or not, or can you not give a definite answer to this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In principle, in principle, this order in this form would not go further from brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, mea culpa. I did not ask for a private session and I started with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I was aware of that, but I thought that you would not mention specifics of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I repent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So you wish us to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you worked for the general headquarters and that you were always kept abreast of all the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. It was as of September 1993 -- or, rather, 16th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But right at the beginning of the war, would you know what was the position of Croat units or, say, HVO, in the Vitez area? Or perhaps a direct question: Were these units encircled, surrounded at some point?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Encircled by Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In early 1992, in the beginning of 1992, there was no need to analyse whether they were surrounded by anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. But let's just talk about the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: We can only talk about the time of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, on the ground and in the maps, some units of both were partly surrounded; that is, a part of Vitez, a part of Busovaca, a part of Kiseljak. But likewise, both of them -- or, rather, they were alternatively semi-encircled or encircled. Now, I would have to show you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, right. But a British officer said that in Old Vitez, Muslim forces were surrounded; around them was the HVO, and the HVO was also surrounded, so that it all looked like that shooting target?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. And there were very many cases of that, in Zepce, in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But what I'm interested in is Vitez. Is that correct? Was that British officer correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, they were all semi-surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, the concentration of HVO troops, apart from Vitez, was there one at Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: The HVOs, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you now, please, look at this large map and show us Vitez and Kiseljak and their location?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Kiseljak is right here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to be --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, this is the larger -- this is an aerial photograph and enlargement, so perhaps it's not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. Never mind, then. Excuse me. So these two places where we had concentrations of HVO forces, was there a road communication between them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then this road which linked the two groupings of HVO forces, if I can put that way, was of strategic importance for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, it depends how you look at it. Yes, it was of strategic importance, and no, it wasn't. But yes, rather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of the military tactics or, rather, strategy, is the separation of enemy forces and then the destruction of individual groups, thus the separating?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. So you see how my Bilic [phoen] training, education is still very active. Well, I spent there ten years, and you learn the tactics quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But let us move on to another question. You did give us an answer to that, but I should like to really lay stress on it, because we saw a film, and your answer -- your response to it will be different than the author's. At the time of the SFRY and the JNA, a reservist took his weapons back home with him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I'm sure about it, and I was with the JNA until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because one of the witnesses for the Prosecution, who made a film and told us that people with weapons were issued with those weapons as reservists and went back with them home?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Now -- but you have to distinguish --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the JNA period.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs were issued them, that is true. I was the head of the brigade staff, and I know that that is true. So I know that this -- I know this to be the truth. But it wasn't the case before 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Muslims, the reservists, did they ever -- were they ever issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. No, never, and we agree on this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croats were issued with those weapons after the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No. That is another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking whether Muslims reservists were issued that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So only the Serbs went back home with their weapons and the others did not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I did write something about this, which were the strategic activities at the territorial-defence level, and I wrote it down, who was issued with what weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I heard, that, but we heard it from a witness, and he was supposed to be an objective witness and yet he presented us with an unobjective fact. Now, as regards the military tactic. Is surprise one of the permissible methods of warfare?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That is one of the principles. The higher degree of surprise, the effect, the results are better. That is natural in combat operations. And everybody tried to do that. Who managed to catch the enemy by surprise, he achieved results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is probably part of the history of warfare, isn't it, because the history of warfare, you also learn about successful surprise tactics that are taught. For instance, the attack of Normandy was one of such cases. And you must have learned?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, those examples of catching the enemy unawares. Something which is a possible example of tactics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your analysis you also dealt on the system of recruitment, of reserve system and the mobilisation system. Could you please tell us: After the military service, after the regular military service, one became a reservist. Now, at the moment when one becomes a reservist, as of that moment that person is a civilian or a military?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That person is a civilian doing his whatever, regular civilian job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Until he is called to join his unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree on that point too. And now, as regards the mobilisation. Very briefly, tell us the types of mobilisation, but very briefly, and then I will give you an example and ask you whether mobilisation is possible in that way.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, right. There is the secret and public mobilisation, so that was the classification, and that is according to one classification. And there is also regular or surprise mobilisation, in part or in whole. I said yesterday how people are called up may vary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. We don't have to go into that. I will give you an example, and that example is from the Bosnia conflict. That is not in a stable -- not from a stable state, which has existed for years; it is summons in an unstable situation for an army which is in the making yet. And is it possible for the military police, if I -- if I seem to be leading, do, please, interrupt me, but perhaps this is the simplest way and we can waste least time. Is it possible that two or three military policemen come to somebody's home, just pick people up and take them to the front line?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a possible solution if a soldier were -- received a summons and failed to respond. So if I got this summons and, however, did not respond, did not report to my unit, and the military police is bound, or whatever is the authority, to come and take me to the -- to my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are referring to the regular state of affairs. But if there was no summons in writing, can then the military police come and pick up people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, that can happen also, but the scope of it and how often it happened, I really don't know. But in practice that is of course possible, simply because in the beginning there was a lot of arbitrariness about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we agree on all the points that we talk about. Very well. Now, I should like the usher to show the witness P135. I have the text in Croatian -- rather, in Bosniak. You see, do you have the Croatian or, rather, the Bosniak text in front you? Well, no, it is Croatian, because of what the document is. It is the Croatian Defence Council. So this is the replenishment of the Vitez Brigade. That is what it is about. What I should like to know is what conclusions would you draw from item 3, 3, which reads: "Between the 16th of April to the 28th of April they were mobilised --" I shall begin at the beginning. "Between the 16th of April until the 28th of April, '93, they mobilised 498 conscripts as a whole and they were actively included in HVO units in addition to the regular personnel of the Vitez Brigade." And now we shall do a full stop here and interpret this sentence. Do you agree that this text seems to indicate that there was a regular crew, if I may call it that, of Vitez Brigade, without people mobilised, and when the war broke out, that this brigade was replenished with reservists? Is that what transpires from this sentence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I could interpret it in two ways. I have nothing against it. I am giving you my interpretation. Well, one way is that the structure of the brigade, in terms of organisation, was below the number of soldiers who were at that point with a brigade. That is, that there were more soldiers in the brigade than would be warranted by its structure. And another interpretation is -- now, what this term was supposed to mean, one would really have to look into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As it says here -- you have the next passage, which perhaps may expand on this. The next sentence says: "The largest number of military conscripts mobilised after the first day of the conflict were immediately included in the first line of defence. They are used as replacements on the lines after the first assault; that is, they are gradually included as replacements for the soldiers from the mobile personnel." Now, could you tell me, does it transpire, clearly from this text, which was -- which part of the army participated in the first strike?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It was the members, the brigade numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but it doesn't say brigade here. It says "replacement for soldiers from the mobile personnel." So is that active? In the former JNA, were they all soldiers under contract, or who were they?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, now, I cannot really say whether those were soldiers under contract, as it says here, because we did not have any professional men in the former JNA, except for that particular category -- a few soldiers are under contract -- and towards the end I believe it was first implemented in practice sometime in 1990 or end of 1990. But now we do not have that particular category of persons and the brigade could not be replenished with those men at that time. I simply think that this was a brigade in the making on the basis of a particular structure or pattern, and it had its subordinate units, which were replenished. But there was a mobilisation; additional mobilisation was carried out because of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, right. So we agree. And now, will you please tell me -- I mean, these are your conjectures, as a matter of fact, because you did not really keep abreast of that --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Really, I do know some things, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let us move onto the Territorial Defence. When was the system of -- when was the chain of command established in the Territorial Defence? Could you give us the time frame?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I don't understand you. What do you mean from below up?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the Territorial Defence -- that is, the commanding and the commanded, did they exist in the Territorial Defence? Was there a chain of command established in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as a wartime unit is mobilised -- and TO units were mostly wartime units, so some of the TO units only had their offices. That is a part of the command which existed in peacetime already, and all the rest were reservists; that is, either reserve soldiers and reserve officers or NCOs. Until the unit -- until such time as when the unit was mobilised, that it fully formed the reserve officer, the reserve had no commanding authority. And after a unit was formed, then there was -- then all this disappeared between an active reserve soldier or an active reserve officer and an active officer or an active duty soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So TO units which then grew into the BH army, were they formed on the basis of the territorial principle; that is, all the inhabitants of a village in one unit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Why, yes. Those units were also formed on the basis of the territorial principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, right. We know what the territorial principle is. I only wanted this to be confirmed. And those units which were formed on the basis of the territorial principle -- that is, one village, one unit, never mind which -- those soldiers or militia men or home guards were put up in special building facilities; that is, barracks with training grounds and whatnot, or did everybody go back home every time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, specifically, I did have an opportunity to see that. And with the HVO in Konjic or Fojnica and other places, Mr. Something, I don't know what his name was, they were using the schools, and as a rule those units would be put up in those schools. Or perhaps some business premises, such as warehouses, those units would be there. But until then, the largest part of the units were at home, that is, at home. But by mid '93 they began to set up branches -- began to set up something else. Well, barracks. Not always proper, true barracks such as in Kiseljak. But there were no barracks. They were at home. As a rule, in schools, or warehouses or in barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were also at home, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what I should like to know next is you said the BH army had considerable trouble with supplies. And this trouble -- did these supplies also cover uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, all the material, resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am interested in uniforms, because uniforms are very important in this regard. I should repeat my question. Was there a shortage of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there was a shortage of uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there such instances when BH army members would wear civilian clothes on front line towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much for your patience. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Susak. Cross-examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. Dzambasovic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Dzambasovic. I am the Defence counsel for Drago Josipovic. Since we were in the same military formation while doing our military service at Tomoglavac, I think we are going to understand each other better. You talked about attack in your expertise, and you say an attack can be carried out from a circular or semi-circular base. Could you please tell me what that means?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: There are different forms of attack. Frontal attack means that an attack is carried frontally. Then an attack from the flanks, that is the attack comes from either the right or the left flank, and it can be either the east or the west in relation to a particular facility. So that's on the flanks. Then also an attack can come from the rear -- well, depending on the situation. If the positions of your unit are such that you can from -- you can carry out an attack from several different points, then that is better. So then if you create an overall picture, you see whether it's a circular or semi-circular base. So you've encircled someone and then from that encirclement you carry out, you launch an attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
