utterances.text: And now in relation to this I am going to put another question to you. Can defence be organised or carried out from a circular or semi-circular basis?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes. If you are encircled and then the combat operation that should follow is a breakthrough through that encirclement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a circular or semi-circular space is used for an attack or a defence, can diversionary units be brought in as well?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If the conditions are right, this can be done in any situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now we've reached the following point: How is a semi-circular line established of attack or of defence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If I could get a piece of paper, I could draw it for you and then everybody could see it. Could I please get a piece of paper? I could draw a diagram for you. What you see on your monitors now is the following: If this is the enemy in the green square, that would be a semi-circular base attack, approximately. If we were now to add the following, that an attack could be carried out from this side too, or from some other side too, then that is an attack from a circular base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please look at the diagram you drew for us once again.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I have a question for you. I can't see the diagram yet. Fine. Look at this arrow that is closer to you. Yes, that's the south. What does this line mean -- no, not south; the arrow down there closer to you. What does this line that you drew denote?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That means the direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the unit. And this semi-circular line, is that a semi-circular or a circular line?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: That is the deployment of units on the ground, and it may differ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I am going to give you an example and you are going to help me understand this. There is a conflict in a village, and this conflict moved one kilometre to the north, for example. And where it originally broke out, this conflict, there were houses, houses that were scattered around, only a few Muslim and Croat houses. Where the Muslim and Croat houses were, those that were scattered about, they are adjacent to a territory where there was no war, no conflict, and then the conflict extends further. How do you interpret this, that not a single Muslim was killed, not a single Croat was killed, and there were even some officers of Bosnia-Herzegovina there; they all remained alive and they were military-aged men? How do you explain this: that in one corner of the village these houses remained intact and that there was no conflict? Is it because of the distance involved? Or if we look at the scattered houses and then on the other part of the -- in the other part of the village where there are many more houses, there is a clearing between the two. So what is your opinion? How did this happen or why did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to answer. Everything you said can be true, and, on the other hand, it need not be true. This can be outside the zone of responsibility. That is one possibility. Then it may be that it was not important, in terms of the assignment, because it is not a significant target. It may be that somebody reached an agreement and said, "We are not going to do anything. Let us go," et cetera, et cetera. So there are several possibilities and every one of them can either be true or untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am laying special emphasis on the fact that nobody got killed, nobody got hurt, nobody was shot on that day from any ethnic group, no houses were torched, nothing happened there.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: If this was within the zone of responsibility, it is strange, but if it is outside the zone of responsibility, it's natural. But now I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you interpret it as follows: that there was less interest involved, less importance, that there should be no conflict there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Whatever you say in this case can be either true or untrue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I am going to move on to another question. As for civilian defence, since the rules were taken over from the former JNA, you said here that civilian protection, civilian defence, was organised in headquarters, units and special representatives. Who was the special representative?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: A special representative was in the local community, this lowest social political community. He was in charge of these particular matters; that is to say, if there was a natural disaster, an earthquake, et cetera, he should mobilise people; that is, that individual who was called in different ways and different places. But this was the lowest level of setting up this civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that that's the lowest level of civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the tasks of the representative for civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: So we are talking about the lowest level; that is to say, two or three villages. So if, from his superior, he receives an order to engage a civilian defence unit, to act as follows: that is to say, to give call-up papers to civilian protection unit members and to set up a unit within this area of civilian protection, and then he should act in accordance with the tasks that he received. So that will be his authority, because that is this lowest level. But then it went further on upwards, towards the municipality, et cetera. There were different levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question. This representative refers to the civilian authorities in the municipality. For example, does he refer to the defence department of Vitez, for example? I mean, in view of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: No, he is not attached to the defence department of Vitez, this representative of the civilian defence. However, civilian defence units carried out tasks for defence purposes, those that were not of a combat nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell me now: In war, or immediately after war, what are the obligations of civilian defence? In the immediate aftermath of a war or, for example, during a war, is one of the tasks to take care of the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Civilian defence units are used for the consolidation of the front line and the terrain. This is an expert notion that is used, an expert term. That is to say, to prevent the outbreak of contagious diseases. And as for the front line, it means taking care of the wounded, of the dead, of persons and animals and buildings. That is to say that if a building was destroyed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one of the tasks is to take care of all the dead bodies that are in that area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's part of their task, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can this be considered to be humane work, since the war had stopped much earlier? If it's no longer a battleground, can this be considered to be a very humane effort? For example, taking care of dead bodies, removing dead bodies, all the things that you mentioned, can this be considered to be a humane effort?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, it's certainly a humane effort if none of this has been taken care of. If there are authorities that are in charge of that, then it's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, let's move on. I'm going to ask you something about war, if there is a conflict, and if one side in a war loses. The side that lost the war, does it surrender its weapons or not, or can an agreement be reached in this respect, how arms would be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Perhaps I did not fully understand you, but I'll try to tell you the following: When combat operations cease, or when a war ends, we believe that one side was defeated, for example. Now, whether it's going to surrender its weapons or not, that depends on international agreements if international factors are involved. So, for example, there is this latest example of Kosovo. KFOR gave a deadline for the Kosovo army to disarm, so that is one way of doing it, how one acts after combat activities cease. If international factors are not involved in the process of peace or of building the peace, then it depends on the internal situation; that is to say, how the military and political leadership is going to act. That's what it depends on, whether somebody is going to hand over their weapons or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it depends on the decisions that will be reached by the two conflicting parties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, my last question would be: Do you know anything about exchanges, either of population, either of one ethnic group or another, at what level this was carried out? Was this done at the level of the military authorities or civilian authorities? And could you tell us at which levels these things were done, the exchange of prisoners of war, civilians, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, that was organised from the top; that is to say, from the level of the state. There were official authorities that were involved in such matters. In practice, in the practice that prevailed, I don't know whether it went to the municipal level or whether specifically -- I don't want to make a mistake. I don't know whether it was the municipal level or lower than that, but there were exchanges that were carried out within units too. For example, you and I reach an agreement, and we do something that we agreed upon. So --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could agreements be reached at the level of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I think so. I don't know any specific examples now, but I think they did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So, for example, the municipalities of Vitez and Zenica, do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you a specific example. I don't know about this. I know that in Blaskic, for example, that somebody from Travnik was in charge of this exchange, but as for this particular case that you mentioned, I cannot give you an answer, because I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzambasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions because they have been exhausted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only wanted to draw your attention to this map which was already tendered. This is a map that was admitted as D9/2, and, therefore, I think it will be unnecessary for us to call in any other experts with this regard. And it's going to be very brief. Since this is the only copy that is here in the courtroom right now, I would like to ask the usher to show the witness this map. And we got this map from the Office of the Prosecutor right now. That is to say that the map that was tendered is not in here right now because it's being photocopied. Cross-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please, could you have a look at this? This is the deployment of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Excuse my interruption for just a moment. Excuse my interruption. I have been advised that this may well have been a document that was introduced or tendered in the course of perhaps closed testimony of a protected witness. In view of, you know, our endeavours to ensure confidentiality in that regard, I'd perhaps just remind my learned friend, and perhaps we could make sure it's handled appropriately now. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It was admitted in open session in the Aleksovski case, and now I cannot remember whether it was in open or closed session in this case, but at any rate, we can move into closed session in this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Private session. Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: 2 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a test. Can you hear me now, Brigadier, or can you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In answer to my learned friend Mr. Radovic you made a remark about the issue of weapons to Croats after the war in Croatia. I would ask you just three questions on that. One, is on what knowledge you base that comment; two, if you know how extensive was that arming of obviously non-active Croat persons; and thirdly, do you know when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. When the war broke out and ended in Croatia, on the basis of the agreement concluded by the republics, a part of the armaments was left behind in the barracks in the Republic of Croatia; that is, part of equipment and armament and Varistine [phoen] and all the other barracks where the conditions were all right. And those armaments and equipment were used to equip the Croatian army and the HVO - that's no secret -- and also the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, all three of them. The weapons, now, how they came by it, I -- I never dealt with logistics in my life, in my professional career, so I don't know. Some were purchased, some papers were seen, and all of the manners -- how did the logistics people manage? I don't know. So that was the beginning and the end of the war in Croatia, and so far then, the Croatian army or, rather, the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the Bosniak Muslims and later on the Muslims, also used some of these armaments and equipment from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think just the last item I asked you is: Do you recall, in terms of the date, when that happened? Can you say in months or weeks as to when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DZAMBASOVIC [RESUMED]
utterances.text: I know specifically when I was in Konjic, from -- HVO command being Dinko Zebic, Ivica Azinovic who cooperated with me. We cooperated closely. They were issuing some papers to individuals who were involved in the purchase or procurement of these weapons. But how they did it in the territorial Republic of Croatia, I really don't know, but I know it was April/May 1992. At that time armaments were arriving from the Republic of Croatia. How, in that way specifically, I really never learned that, but, you know that -- it was a regular occurrence and that was no secret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And I'm obliged to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. We don't have any questions for the witness. Brigadier Dzambasovic, thank you so much for testifying as an expert witness. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we move on to our next witness, I would like to tell you how we intend to plan for our future sittings. We very much hope that by Thursday of next week we may finish with the evidence, both the rebuttal witnesses and any rejoinder witnesses, as you know. Then closing arguments will be held in November, the 8th, the 9th, and the 10th of November. You also know that we have already set deadlines for the submissions of written briefs. You may submit either, say, an outline of your closing arguments with references to relevant parts of transcripts or, if you wish, you may submit a fully-fledged written brief on both legal and factual issues. As for the oral arguments, we thought that we would allocate 3 hours and 45 minutes to the Prosecution -- this would be Monday, the 8th of November -- an hour and a half to each Defence counsel, except for the Defence counsel of Dragan Papic. There's only Count 1, and he would be allocated one hour. So 1 hour and 30 minutes for all the Defence counsel, for a total of 8 hours and 30 minutes. Of course, Defence Counsel Slokovic-Glumac and Radovic, they can decide how to share the 3 hours. You have together 3 hours. It's for you to decide whether each of you will use an hour and a half or otherwise. But that means that for that purpose, we would have to sit on the 9th and the 10th of November from 8.30 in the morning to 1.30. From 8.30 to 1.30. Only in this way could we have 8 hours and 30 minutes available for Defence counsel. I hope these arrangements are suitable. What about the Prosecution? So you would have three -- all of Monday morning, for a total of 3 hours and 45 minutes, because we exclude the breaks, two breaks, one 30-minute break and one 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no comments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And Defence counsel? I see you don't have any objection. Of course, it is a maximum. If you speak for less than an hour and a half, it's even better. More so because there's no point in repeating what you may have already put on paper in your written briefs. So we plan, therefore, to finish on the 10th of November by 1.30, and then we will start deliberations. We very much hope to deliver our judgement in January. If you are not too tired, we could now move on and call the next witness. Do you want a 10-minute break? Would you prefer a 10-minute break? No break. Let's go on. Depending on the interpreters because, of course -- I hope the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It might be good to have a break. It's extremely hot in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We have already complained twice against the warmth, but the technicians don't seem to pay any attention to our requests. So let's have a 10-minute break. So we resume at quarter to one and go on until 1.30.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The expert witness's testimony will be D41/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the following witness asked for protective measures, which would be a closed session and the granting of a pseudonym, and the defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right, then, the blinds should be drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I take advantage of the time needed to bring the witness in to present the Prosecution's position about the documents that Mrs. Slokovic-Glumac suggested on Monday? I am talking about documents which -- affidavits which reveal the personality of the accused, Kupreskic, and which were given the number D29/1. The Prosecution has no objections at all to those documents being submitted as evidence. But, as regards those documents which were numbered D31/1, I would make the following comment: In the documents, we find in the first place there are documents which relate to incidents that -- incidents of the witness Sakib Ahmic's particular life, and in particular incidents which occurred in '71 and in '79. The Prosecution has no objection to those documents which relate to the professional life of the witness Sakib Ahmic be tendered as evidence for the Tribunal. But the other evidence relate to divorce proceedings which took place in 1985 and which was granted in 1986 by a judgement for which we do not have a translation. As regards those documents which deal with the divorce proceedings, I refer to the -- to Rule 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, protect the privacy of a witness, and the documents which relate to the divorce proceedings have absolutely no relationship --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just say something? This document was not included in our proposals because it is a private document, but it's not the only reason. The witness, on several occasions, in response to the questions related to the divorce, it is obvious that there were problems between him and his wife, and that alcohol was the problem and that there were beatings, et cetera. So, in response to direct questions, this is related to medical documents that were submitted, whether this witness knew why he was beaten up and why he spent 17 days in hospital. He said that he did not know. But it is obvious from these records that he was beaten up by his sons. It is not that we want to go into the private life of the witness, but in response to the direct questions put by the defence, he gave false answers. So that is the only reason why we are questioning his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like the sketch that the previous witness made to be admitted into evidence. That is the sketch relating to attack and defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It has already been admitted into evidence. There's even a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document was tendered. It's D41/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We consider that those documents relating to the proceedings of Mr. Sakib Ahmic are not relevant, so they will not be admitted into evidence. The other ones will be admitted into evidence. I see your point, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac; however, we feel that it's -- they are not relevant. So we can move on to -- so closed session and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: at 1.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of September, 1999 at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
